figures.caption: Figure 1: MAS-BIT combines neural and phonetic evidence through specialized experts and an arbiter. (A) Two BIT-initialized encoders process each recording through participant-specific input projections. Fused hidden states condition the neural expert and arbiter; both phoneme posteriors condition the phonetic expert. All three language agents share a frozen text backbone with separate adapters. (B) Each expert replays its greedy draft to construct latent messages from probability-weighted token embeddings. Zr denotes its input, ZN or ZP , and er identifies the message source. The arbiter loss trains active upstream components through these latent messages. (C) Five-epoch alignment, encoder adaptation, and specialization stages precede 40 epochs of joint optimization. Filled cells indicate parameter updates; frozen downstream weights retain input gradients.

Table 1: Published end-to-end benchmark results. Values are corpus WER (%); Feng et al. (2024) and BIT scores follow Zhang et al. (2026). MoDAl reports mean ± 95% CI over five seeds; MoDAl-Full also uses area 44. BrainWhisperer-cross uses additional neural datasets. ∗T15 public/private subset unspecified. – denotes an unreported result.

Figure 2: Jointly trained multi-agent decoding achieves state-of-the-art end-to-end performance. (A) Published BIT end-to-end results (Zhang et al., 2026) and MAS-BIT on T12 holdout and T15 public. (B) Blue curves use the released participant-specific BIT encoders; purple curves use the corresponding fine-tuned encoder branch and final phoneme readout from MAS-BIT. Both cascades use the same WFST, unpruned 5-gram, and OPT rescoring settings at the 13 measured candidate limits; green lines show MAS-BIT. Gray diamonds at K = 100 mark the published BIT cascade results on T12 and T15 public. All panels report corpus holdout WER (%, lower is better); candidate limits use a logarithmic axis.

Figure 3: Expert specialization and latent communication improve end-to-end decoding. (A) Role-specific prompts; # marks the continuous-input slot. (B–C) T12 and T15 holdout WER; solid and hatched bars show T15 public and private. The eight controls and rank-24 single-agent variant share the backbone and two-encoder initialization. The Borealis-5B single-agent variant uses a 4B decoder with rank-13 LoRA; all single-agent variants receive both input views. Bars have the same zero-origin scale. (D) Selected validation transcripts show the arbiter matching a correct expert and recovering sentences when both drafts are wrong. Expert errors are red; corresponding correct arbiter words are green.

Table 3: Prompts for MAS-BIT and all ablation controls. The placeholder # is replaced by the continuous input in the middle column. Paired text delimiters and instruction text are shown verbatim. Each template is a single line; line breaks are typographic.
Table 4: Parameter groups updated in each stage. The pretrained language-model backbone remains frozen throughout.

Table 6: Word positions correct in exactly one expert draft. Columns identify the correct expert; substitution/deletion counts describe the other expert’s error. Training frequency is measured in the pooled neural fine-tuning transcripts. Phoneme distance is averaged over dictionary-covered substitutions, with coverage shown explicitly.

Table 7: Arbitration is most accurate with both expert messages and direct neural conditioning. Word edits, corpus validation WER (%), and exact sentence matches cover all 880/1,426 T12/T15 utterances and 5,496/9,445 reference words. All conditions use fixed weights, FP32 batch-one decoding, and the same cached expert outputs. Complete-input predictions match the preceding arbitration analysis and the Top-16 message condition.

Figure 5: Token alternatives improve decoding in both participants. Changes in corpus validation WER are relative to top-16 messages at τ = 1 on all 880 T12 and 1,426 T15 validation utterances. Positive values indicate higher WER. Token support varies from 1 to 16 on a logarithmic axis. Values are labeled to three decimals. Model weights, expert drafts, direct neural input, and greedy arbiter decoding remain fixed.

Table 13: Reported neural-to-text decoding on author-defined evaluation sets. Values are WER (%) as reported. Fiedler et al. report best runs with full fine-tuning. Olak et al. report mean ± SD over five seeds; MoDAl values are mean ± 95% CI over five seeds.

Table 15: Candidate-sentence counts and holdout decoding. Values are WER (%); T15 public and private scores refer to separate subsets. K is the candidate-sentence limit in our reproduced cascade using either the released BIT encoder or MAS-BIT’s fine-tuned participant-specific encoder branch and phoneme readout; BIT + LightBeam uses the released BIT encoders. Blue shading marks MAS-BIT.

Table 16: Holdout performance of MAS-BIT and its ablations. Values are WER (%) on the same hidden holdouts. The five core controls, the rank-24 single-agent variant, the sequential dual-view refinement control, the detached-latent-message control, and the message-only arbiter control use the shared backbone, two-encoder frontend, and checkpoint-selection protocol; the Borealis-5B single-agent variant replaces the 1.7B decoder with a 4B audio-trained decoder and rank-13 adapter.

Figure 6: Joint training aligns the neural interface while preserving distinct expert views. (A) Pooled ZN– audio/text RSA before and after training. (B) Encoder-branch alignment with the audio reference; native and cross-participant branches are defined by the input participant and encoder origin. (C) Within-model RSA between encoder branches before/after training, and between the two expert input views in the two-neural-expert control and MAS-BIT. Points and intervals are word-count-stratified estimates and pointwise 95% sentencebootstrap intervals. Audio references use the 0.6B Qwen audio tower on fixed-voice TTS; text references use the 1.7B text decoder.
